title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Runbooks (Comprehensive Reference)
author: Asha Patel
content:
Overview:

This document is a single-source reference for Redwood Inference's serving runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling/playbooks, benchmarking suite, recent release notes, known issues, operational runbooks, and team wiki links. It is intended for SREs, runtime engineers, infra, and applied ML engineers who operate or optimize inference capacity.

Goals:
- Describe runtime architecture and design trade-offs
- Provide prescriptive kernel scheduling and configuration guidelines
- Share profiling playbooks and sampling procedures for performance investigations
- Document the canonical benchmarking harness and expected baselines
- Surface recent runtime release notes and known issues impacting customers
- Include runbooks for common incidents and operational tasks

1) High-level Architecture

Summary:
The serving runtime is a modular, GPU-optimized inference engine that supports continuous batching, KV cache management, quantization-aware execution paths, and dynamic kernel selection. The control plane routes requests, applies routing policy, and coordinates caching/batching decisions. The data plane runs on dedicated worker pools (hosted) or customer-managed nodes (private).

Components (logical):
- API Gateway: ingress, auth, rate limits, request validation.
- Router/Dispatcher: routes requests to pools by policy (latency-first, cost-first, region, tier).
- Runtime Worker: process that executes model inference, manages KV cache, executes kernels. Each worker binds one or more CUDA contexts and manages GPU memory pools.
- Batch Coordinator: merges compatible requests into micro-batches respecting sequence-length SLOs and token budgets.
- Cache Service: prefix/KV cache with TTLs and LRU eviction; local hot-cache on worker for low-latency reuse.
- Telemetry/Tracing: per-request trace with token-level timings exported to observability backend.

Key design decisions and tradeoffs:
- Continuous batching reduces cost but increases tail latency under highly variable loads. We use policy-driven batch-timeouts (default 8ms, 16ms when >90% utilization).
- Kernel selection is dynamic: a kernel selector evaluates model type, dtypes, sequence length, batch size, and selects the fastest tested kernel for the GPU/HW.
- KV cache is sharded per-worker to avoid cross-host synchronization; global cache hints are used for cross-worker warmup.

2) Kernel Scheduling and Selection

Objective:
Maximize throughput while meeting per-route latency SLOs and memory constraints.

Kernel selection heuristics (applied in order):
1. Prefer fused attention kernels for transformers when sequence length < 2k and model supports them.
2. Use int8/quatized kernels for large context models when quality regressions are within threshold for the workload (quality budget).
3. Fall back to FP16 kernels for compatibility or for sequence lengths with no optimized fused kernels.
4. Use NVTE/other vendor kernels for specific GPUs when they outperform default runtime kernels in regression tests.

Scheduling rules (examples):
- Latency-sensitive routes: set max_batch_size = 4, batch_timeout = 4ms, preferring kernels with lower startup overhead.
- Throughput-first routes: set max_batch_size = 64, batch_timeout = 20ms, prefer large-batch kernels that utilize cuBLAS/cuDNN fused ops.
- Mixed workloads: use request tagging and the Router to pin latency-sensitive traffic onto pools configured with smaller batch sizes and preloaded models.

Operator knobs and config snippet (example YAML):
```
runtime_pool:
  name: latency-pool-us-west
  gpu_type: A100-80GB
  max_batch_size: 8
  batch_timeout_ms: 8
  prefer_kernels: ["fused-attn-v2", "fp16-default"]
  kv_cache_local: true
  quantization_profile: "int8-cautious"
```

3) Profiling Playbook (step-by-step)

When investigating a perf regression or high tail latency, follow this playbook. Each step has a target outcome and owner.

1) Reproduce and scope (SRE/Runtime SME)
- Collect failing requests (trace IDs) and time bounds.
- Re-run requests against staging with identical model/version and input distribution.
- Outcome: reproduce latency/tail behavior in an isolated environment.

2) Capture golden traces (runtime engineer)
- Enable detailed per-token latency tracing for the request(s).
- Commands: `rd-runner --trace=token --trace-output=/tmp/trace.json --request-id=<id>`
- Outcome: identify which layer/kernel contributes to tail.

3) GPU-level profiling (runtime engineer)
- Use nsight systems / nvprof or CUPTI-based lightweight sampling.
- Example: `nsys profile -o /tmp/profile --trace=cuda,osrt rd-worker --model my-model`
- Inspect kernel launch times, memcpy, and kernel stalls.

4) Kernel microbenchmarks (runtime/benchmarking)
- Run microbench for suspect kernels: `bench-kernel --kernel fused-attn-v2 --seq-len 1024 --batch 8 --gpu A100`
- Compare against known baseline table (see Benchmarking section).

5) Memory/fragmentation checks (infra)
- Check GPU memory fragmentation with `nvidia-smi -q` and runtime allocator metrics.
- If fragmentation is >40% and OOMs are observed, restart worker with jumbo slab sizes or enable defragmentation heuristic.

6) Rollback or mitigation (owner: oncall/runtime lead)
- Mitigation options: pin kernel to older vendor kernel, reduce batch sizes, enable model-level cache, or rollback runtime version.
- Follow the Runbook for kernel pinning below.

4) Benchmarking Suite and Expected Baselines

Benchmark harness overview:
- The harness (bench-suite) supports: latency P99/P95, throughput at target tokens/sec, peak memory, kernel microbenchmarks, and regression tests for quality (perplexity/ROUGE on sample prompts).
- Harness produces JSON reports with machine metadata, kernel versions, and workloads.

Canonical benchmark workloads:
- chat-short: typical conversational requests (avg tokens 64, max 512)
- long-context-qa: long context documents (avg 2048, max 8192)
- batch-embed: high-throughput embedding workload (avg tokens 1, batch 128)

Baseline targets (A100-80GB, int8-cautious profile):
- chat-short: p50 = 18ms, p95 = 42ms, p99 = 78ms (per-token time ~0.9ms)
- long-context-qa: p50 = 210ms, p95 = 420ms, p99 = 800ms
- batch-embed (b=128): throughput = 75k tokens/sec, p95 < 60ms

Running the suite (example):
```
bench-suite run --config profiles/a100-int8-cautious.yaml --workloads chat-short,long-context-qa --report /tmp/report.json
```

Interpreting results:
- Compare kernel versions in report to baseline table. If throughput drops >15% for the same kernel+cfg, mark a regression and open a ticket with the runtime-kernel label.

5) Recent Release Notes (summary)
- 2026-02-28: runtime v3.4.1 — Added fused-attn-v2 kernel, lowered default batch_timeout to 8ms for latency pools, improved KV cache warmup heuristics.
- 2026-01-15: runtime v3.3.0 — Added int8 quantization pipeline, opt-in; improved allocator fragmentation heuristics.
- 2025-11-02: runtime v3.2.4 — Stability fixes for model reloads and host-side GC improvements.

Upgrade guidance:
- Canary deploy: deploy new runtime to a small subset of latency pools (5% traffic) for 48 hours, run bench-suite smoke tests and production shadow traffic checks.
- Full rollout: follow the rollout checklist in the Runbook section.

6) Known Issues (operational)

ISSUE-001: Intermittent P99 spikes on mixed pools when utilization > 85%
- Symptom: P99 latency > 2x baseline during sustained high QPS.
- Root cause: batching queue head-of-line blocking when large batch kernels are prioritized.
- Mitigation: enable per-route small-batch reservation or reduce default max_batch_size.
- Status: mitigated by config change in 2026-02-28 release.

ISSUE-002: Occasional OOMs after long-running model reloads
- Symptom: worker OOMs within 24-48 hours of continuous reloads.
- Root cause: allocator fragmentation on some drivers + small slab sizes.
- Mitigation: increase slab size and enable defrag in runtime config.

ISSUE-003: Quality degradation with aggressive int8 profile on chat-long workloads
- Symptom: measured ROUGE/perplexity regression > acceptable threshold on some prompt-sets.
- Mitigation: restrict int8 profile to batch-embed and non-chat routes; require per-model quality gate.

7) Runbooks (playbooks for common operational tasks)

Runbook: High P99 latency (owner: eng-sre)
1. Triage: pull p95/p99 by route and pool.
2. Isolate pool: remove pool from Router via `routerctl drain-pool <pool>` (5m grace).
3. Reproduce and profile on staging; run profiling playbook steps 1-4.
4. If kernel regression suspected: pin kernel via `runtime-config set pool.<pool>.prefer_kernels=["fp16-default"]` and monitor for 15m.
5. Rollback runtime if mitigation fails.

Runbook: Worker OOM / crash loop (owner: eng-infra)
1. Check logs: `rd-logs tail <worker-id> --lines 500`.
2. Inspect allocator metrics and fragmentation.
3. Temporarily increase OOM margin: `runtime-config set worker.<id>.slab_base_mb=1024`.
4. Schedule rolling restart with drained traffic.

Runbook: Model rollback (owner: runtime-team)
1. Pin traffic to previous model version: `routerctl set-route-model <route> <model-id>@<version>`
2. Initiate model unload on new workers: `runtime-admin unload-model --id <model-id> --force`.
3. Monitor traces for 30-60m.

9) Ownership, SLAs and SLOs

Owners:
- Runtime core: eng-serving-runtime (rotation: oncall-runtime)
- Benchmarks & QA: applied-ml-and-evals
- Infra / GPU fleet: eng-infra

SLOs (example):
- Route-level p95 latency SLO: 500ms (critical routes), error budget 99.9%
- Worker uptime SLO: 99.95% per month
- Benchmark regression detection: detect >10% throughput drop at p95 baseline within 24h

10) Appendices

A. Example kernel microbenchmark invocation
```
bench-kernel --kernel fused-attn-v2 --gpu A100-80GB --seq-len 1024 --batch 8 --iters 200
```

B. Useful CLI references
- routerctl: manage routing pools and route assignments
- runtime-config: change pool/worker-level runtime knobs
- rd-runner: local request replayer and tracer
- bench-suite: internal benchmarking harness

C. Contact and escalation
- Runtime oncall Slack: #runtime-oncall
- Pager: eng-runtime-pager (pager duty)
- Escalation: runtime lead -> infra lead -> eng-sre manager -> CTO

Document history: major changes are tracked in the release notes page and in the changelog. For any edits to kernel selection logic or production defaults, open an ADR in architecture-and-standards and link to that ADR in related_pages.

End of document.
